newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Protests mar opening of Taiwan's National Assembly.
newsitem.headline: Protests mar opening of Taiwan's National Assembly.

text.p: Taiwan's National Assembly kicked off a two-month session to amend the constitution on a chaotic note on Monday as politicians both in and out of parliament staged demonstrations against government policy.
Riot police scuffled with some 50 protesters from the radical Taiwan Independence Party, none of them assembly members, to block their way into the building.
The protesters, shouting "Institute a Taiwan Republic constitution" and "the Republic of China is eating up Taiwan," said the proposed amendments were misguided.

"We don't need a revision of the constitution. We only want a constitution for the Taiwan Republic," said Stephen Lee, secretary-general and protest organiser for the party, which espouses independence from China.
Taiwan's Republic of China government, set up by the Nationalists after they lost a civil war on the mainland in 1949, says it eventually wants to re-unify with China.
President Lee Teng-hui convened the assembly, one of Taiwan's two branches of parliament and responsible for revising the constitution, to discuss constitutional issues.
One of the proposed amendments sought to give the president the powers to appoint the premier and decide major policies without consent from the law-making branch of the parliament.
Protesters from the right-wing New Party marched to the assembly holding up banners bearing the signatures of residents protesting the government's failure to check a recent string of violent crimes.
The protesters, who were allowed to enter because they were assembly members, shouted into loudspeakers and staged a sit-in at the assembly podium to try to stall the assembly's opening.
"What's the point of revising the constitution when we can't even maintain our social order?" said Yang Shih-hsiung, a New Party deputy.
Taiwan people were shocked and grief-stricken after police found the body of Pai Hsien-yen, the kidnapped daughter of actress Pai Ping-ping, floating naked in a river on April 28.
The kidnappers, who remain at large, had strangled the 17-year-old with rope, bound her hands and sunk her in the river with weights.
The gruesome murder was the latest in a spate of violent crimes that have hit Taiwan since November.
Last November two gunmen broke into the home of magistrate Liu Pang-yu and killed eight people, including Liu.
One week later, women's rights activist Peng Wan-ju was raped and stabbed to death in southern Kaohsiung. Police found 35 knife wounds in her naked body.
Around 50,000 people demonstrated on Sunday and staged an all-night vigil outside Taipei's Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall to protest against the island's worsening crime levels.
The New Party later tried to endorse a proposal calling for the resignation of Vice President Lien Chan, who doubles as premier, for failing to improve social order.
